result:
You have 1000 words. That's not a lot. Or maybe it's an incredible amount.

1000 words is three double-spaced pages. It's a 7-minute speech. It's the length of an apology that actually means something. It's also nothing at all - a single news article you scroll past, a chapter you'd skip.

So what do you do with a thousand of them?

I could tell you a story. I think I will.

There was a kid who collected jars.

Not seashells, not stamps. Jars. Empty jam jars, pickle jars, old peanut butter jars that even after ten washes still smelled faintly of peanuts. He kept them on a shelf in his room, and people thought it was weird but harmless, which is the best kind of weird to be when you're twelve.

His mother asked him once why.

"To put things in," he said.

"What things?"

"Things I don't want to forget."

She nodded like she understood, but she didn't. Not yet.

He started small. A blue marble he found on the playground that he was convinced was lucky. A folded-up note from his best friend that said *secret club meeting at 3 - don't be late!!!* He stopped being invited to secret club meetings about a year later, but the note stayed.

Then he got more ambitious.

He tried to catch air.

He would go outside on really good days - the kind of October day where the light is golden and low and everything looks like it's forgiving you - and he would just stand there with an open jar and then screw the lid on fast.

He labeled that one: *Sunday, October 9th, 4:32 PM. Perfect.*

His sister made fun of him. "That's just air, idiot. That's not anything."

But he kept it.

He had a jar for the first snow. Not the snow itself, because that melted and just became sad jar water. But he put in a little pine branch that had snow on it, and when the snow melted he left the branch. *First Snow.*

He had a jar of beach sand from a trip that wasn't fun at all, where his parents fought the whole drive home. He kept the sand anyway, because it was true.

By the time he was sixteen, the shelf was full. Jars crowded together, dusty, their labels curling at the edges in his messy handwriting. Some of the things inside had changed. Leaves had crumbled. Colors had faded.

His mother came in one day while he was doing homework and said, "We need that shelf for storage. You're too old for this now."

He didn't argue. He took the jars down, one by one, and put them in a cardboard box in the closet. He told himself he'd deal with it later.

He didn't. He went to college. He moved.

Years passed. Apartments, jobs, a life that kept accelerating whether he wanted it to or not.

When he was 34, his mother called. "We're clearing out your old room. Do you want this box of... jars? Or should we throw it away?"

He drove home that weekend. The box was exactly as he left it.

He opened it on the floor of his childhood bedroom, which was now painted a very adult greige and had a Peloton in the corner. He opened the first jar: *Sunday, October 9th, 4:32 PM. Perfect.*

It was just air. Just a jar of air.

He held it up to the light. And for a second - just a breath - he remembered exactly how that air felt. Cool on his cheeks. The smell of leaves. The sound of his sister yelling for him to come inside for dinner but not yet wanting to go.

He cried. Not big, dramatic sobbing. Just tears that came without asking.

Because he realized what he'd been doing.

He wasn't trying to save perfect days. He was trying to learn how to notice them while they were happening.

We all do this, don't we? We take photos of food we won't remember eating. We scribble down quotes we'll never re-read. We tell ourselves "I'll remember this forever" precisely because some quiet part of us knows we won't. Not really. Not the texture of it.

We are all kids with jars, screwing lids onto moments made of air.

So here's what I want to tell you, with my little pile of 1000 words:

You don't need a better jar.

You don't need a perfect memory, or a better camera, or a journaling habit that finally sticks. You just need to pause, for three seconds, in the middle of a perfectly ordinary moment, and notice it.

Notice the weight of the mug in your hand. The way the light is falling right now across whatever room you're in. The faint hum of the fridge or the traffic outside. This. This exact second, which has never happened before and will never happen again, and which will be gone by the time you finish this sentence.

There. You caught it.

We do not get eternity. We get a series of nows, each one light enough to slip through our hands. My job, if I have one in these 1000 words, is not to impress you. It's to remind you to look up.

And if you're wondering about the man? He didn't throw the jars away. He emptied them. He washed them clean, and he put one empty jar on his kitchen counter in his own apartment.

His wife asked him what it was for.

He said, "To put things in."

She understood.

So if you have an empty jar - a shelf, a pocket, a corner of your mind that's still clear - keep it. Keep it empty on purpose. Let it remind you to pay attention.

Because somewhere, right now, someone is breathing October air and not even knowing it's perfect.

Now you know.

You have about 40 words left, if you've been counting. I haven't. I'll waste them the best way I know how:

Thank you for being here. Thank you for reading this far. Go easy on yourself today. Drink some water. Text someone you love.

Your moment is waiting.
